definition: Calm and relaxed, seeming not to worry or get excited about something.
example: With a nonchalant wave, the chef flipped the omelet without even looking at the pan.
nuance: Nonchalant describes an outward air of easy calm that may hide real feelings, while indifferent means someone truly does not care.
prompt: A goalkeeper faces a penalty kick in the final minute of a championship game.
options: Despite the roaring crowd, the goalkeeper looked nonchalant as she adjusted her gloves.
The goalkeeper felt so nonchalant that her knees shook and her breathing turned ragged.
The nonchalant leap required every ounce of the goalkeeper's frantic, straining effort.
The referee measured the nonchalant distance from the penalty spot to the goal line.
reasons: Appearing relaxed and unbothered under heavy pressure fits the word exactly.
Shaking knees and ragged breathing show nerves, the reverse of easy calm.
Frantic straining clashes with the word's sense of effortless, unhurried ease.
A distance has no attitude; the word describes a person's manner, not a length.

practice.prompt: A student learns that his class presentation has been moved up to today.
options: Jamal stayed nonchalant, flipping through his note cards as if nothing had changed.
Jamal grew nonchalant, pacing the hallway and begging the teacher for one more day.
Jamal let out a nonchalant scream of panic when his lab partner shared the news.
The new schedule was nonchalant, so the presentation now started at nine o'clock.
reasons: Calmly carrying on after surprising news shows a relaxed, unworried manner.
Pacing and begging signal panic, which is the opposite of looking unconcerned.
A scream of panic cannot be casual and composed at the same time.
A schedule cannot feel calm; the word fits people and their behavior, not timetables.
